text: The crossing holds because neither arm leans; the dough rises because no hand hurries it. What they share is a kind of waiting that is not passive — both are held in balance by something that cannot be pushed. Press the dough and it tightens; lean on one arm of the crossing and the middle moves. The meeting and the rising are the same patience wearing two shapes.

Where the two paths cross, someone has set a board down on the stone and left dough on it to rise. It takes the hours it takes, and neither path can lend it any. The middle holds while the bread comes up — the weight on both arms unchanged, the warmth working underneath.

Two arms reach from opposite ends and hold their meeting; the pond holds its surface and asks nothing. Both are a stillness that is not emptiness — something is being kept in place by what does not move. Where the crossing keeps its balance by equal reaching, the ice keeps its by not reaching at all. One holds by giving, the other by withholding.

The crossing has iced over at the middle. Both arms still reach the same distance into it, and the ice holds where they meet, asking nothing of either side. Under the surface nothing has gone anywhere. The weight is still equal; it has only stopped moving.

The crossing gives equal weight from both sides; the hedge takes a cost from everything that passes. Between them lies the question of what a passage is worth. Where two arms meet without either taking more, the thorn insists that nothing crosses free. The one is an exchange agreed, the other an exchange extracted.

A thorn hedge has grown up the middle where the two paths meet. Both arms still reach it evenly, and both pay the same to come through — a sleeve, a knuckle, some small tearing. The middle is not closed. It only keeps its price the same from either side.

Two arms reach deliberately toward a middle; water reaches nothing and still arrives. The relation is in the finding — one meeting is made, the other is discovered. Where the crossing needs two to hold it, the slope needs only itself. What they have in common is that neither is forced; what divides them is whether anyone chose.

Water has found the middle where the paths cross and is running through it, taking the slope it was always going to take. The two arms hold their places on either side and the water passes between them, level with both. No one showed it the way in. It leaves by the low ground.
